title: Recording for Columbia and Victor, and acoustic recording methods
summary: He describes the failed Columbia session, the Victor sessions with an eight-inch horn, and how many takes were cut.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Could you I hate to interrupt you again But as you go along Could you give me the details on the records you made I'd like to hear about the What you did for Columbia and how that happened Well on the Columbia

Max Hart fixed a date for us to go up there and make a record Now this place was located at 16 Broadway It was only a block away from Rides and Rambus We went up there one morning to record And they told us to play over the piece And when they did that They were all putting their hands to their ears Some was in the back hitting on hammers Making noises They didn't care to put us in the right position And they'd taken two lousy records And they paid us $250 for nothing For Indiana and Docktown Stutters Ball We recorded for them It was in January about the 27th or 28th But after all greets Shall I tell you again We were actually run out of the place They didn't give us a chance to even get our instruments To give us a check And out we went They was booing us and beating on hammers and laughing at us That music was by beyond their comprehension They didn't take the time To even give us a break to make a good record Victor was it After the tremendous success that we had created Rides and Rambus The Victor Company approaches There were more Patients They had more patience with us They set us up In the hardest way of playing that I've ever played in my life We played into an eight inch horn That is the diameter of the outside horn The horn could have been about three foot long And it was eight inches in diameter And out of that came a little horn about four inches in diameter Where Larry was to play And I stood back about 20 to 25 feet The drummer was alongside of me He was not supposed to use the bass drum because it would break up the wax Or the matrix Dig holes in it And ruin it All he could play was in between like You know like the licks in between He could do that And he played mostly on the kettle drum And on the wood blocks and bells Now this is the hardest way in the world of playing music Of having musicians separated Because when musicians are put together like they record today You can feel one another You can almost know what the other man is going to do By the feel I don't know It's a certain feeling you get When you're playing music You feel the other man's actions and his reactions To what you're going to do Me standing at 20 to 25 feet It was about 15 feet from the horn And Larry stood about four feet from his little horn And the piano was facing me Direct under the horn Now they had a white light A white light was going And that's when they changed You're supposed to watch the light up there And the red light would come on And each man was the count mainly two And we started It's beyond me How we ever started together I don't know But it looks like God was with us Because we always started together I was in the back of them They could hear me But I couldn't hear them Now there was no way of me I've thrown in an extra lick here or there Because if I did And I missed out That matrix was ruined And the whole thing was ruined It's not like the rubber-lipped men played today They play a chorus None of them takes the chorus I'm not criticizing their plan But these rubber-lipped men couldn't even play them These recordings that we played In the position that we played it They play with electric process He can play as slow and easy as he wants And in the booth this man raises the volume up

to make it equal to the other. There was no reason of volume here. You hear the cut or be cut down with the Dixieland Jazz Band. And I believe that's what gave us the edge on all of it because there was no time that I'd ever have to take down on any record record when it went 12 hours. I could still hold that heart in my mouth and play it. Now this might be bragging, but I did it many times. Till the dancers toppled over, I'd stayed in playing. One after the other, until the manager was making stuff. That's the kind of clientele we had at Rice with us. They were all rich people. They liked it. They went for it. We brought it out of the casino courts, which was a dive, you may as well say. Excuse me for interrupting you, but how many matrices,
how many times would you cut a tune? I'll put it that way, because I can't pronounce anything.

Well, we'd play a test record over once. See what I mean a test? And then go through that. Then we'd start on a real matrix. We may make two, three, sometimes four. But not more than three or four of each tune. And we made as high as sometimes three times in a cell. And that's actually almost a nice plan, right there.
